newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland hails NATO moves, sees Moscow stance change.
newsitem.headline: Poland hails NATO moves, sees Moscow stance change.

text.p: Poland's defence ministry on Wednesday welcomed NATO's assurance that it did not intend to station nuclear arms on the soil of future members and said Moscow's views on NATO enlargement were evolving.

Deputy minister Andrzej Karkoszka welcomed a pledge in the final communique of Tuesday's NATO ministerial meeting in Brussels, that alliance states had no intention, plan or reason to station nuclear weapons on the territory of future members.
"We are very pleased with the formulation," Karkoszka told a news conference.
NATO's 16 foreign ministers called an enlargement summit for next July in Madrid at which it will invite some former Soviet bloc states to join, despite Russia's opposition.
Poland, the largest and strategically most sensitive of the leading candidates, which escaped Soviet domination in 1989, expects to be among the first countries to be invited.

Warsaw has stressed that it wants to be a full member and that its rights and responsibilities in the pact should not be diluted because of pressure from Russia, which argues that Polish NATO entry would be a threat to its security.

Karkoszka said the NATO communique made clear that there would be no change in the pact's current nuclear posture, adding that it was essential that the entry of Poland and other states to NATO should not lead to heightened tension in Europe.
In a letter congratulating new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski applauded this week's NATO moves as further progress away from the Cold War era.

"By enlarging the North Atlantic Alliance to the countries of Central Europe and strengthening NATO's relations with Russia, Ukraine and other partner nations, the achievements of recent years will be consolidated," Kwasniewski said.
Karkoszka said the fact that Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was talking to NATO in Brussels showed that Moscow's approach was changing.
Primakov on Wednesday told NATO counterparts Moscow was ready to enter dialogue on a new relationship with the pact which could take the form of a special charter or treaty.

"I think the Russian position will evolve and I expect it will be understood in Russia that there are more gains to be made from cooperation with NATO, than problems and difficulties over its expansion," Karkoszka said.

He was speaking after a Warsaw seminar of defence ministry representatives from NATO and eight central and east European countries, including Russia, on the evolution of their defence strategies in the light of NATO's planned expansion.
Senior Polish General Stanislaw Koziel, who organised the seminar, said he did not expect Russia's current defence strategy priorities to change in response to NATO enlargement.
"Russian experts realise that NATO does not pose a threat to them," Koziel told the news conference.
